title: A predictive decoder for the regulatory genome

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reliable quantitative decoder that predicts how DNA sequence regulates molecular activity in a specified cellular context. Given a genome or a set of sequence changes, together with the cell type, state and conditions to be modeled, it would predict which genes change their expression, how RNA splicing changes and how associated chromatin measurements respond. AlphaGenome provides a substantial technical foundation for this goal, but the broad capability described here has not been demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

Proposed scope: The decoder would connect nearby and distant regulatory elements to their molecular consequences and predict effects in previously unseen individual genomes. It would also handle structural variants and combinations of variants, including cases where their joint effect differs from the sum of their separate effects. Those latter capabilities remain explicit targets of this concept; the supplied evidence does not establish their performance or demonstrate that no existing method can address them. Cellular context is part of the prediction specification, rather than an outcome assumed to be uniquely determined by sequence.

significance.text: If broadly reliable, this capability would make much of the noncoding genome functionally interpretable: researchers could predict which genes a regulatory change affects, in which contexts and by how much. Integrating expression, splicing and chromatin predictions could help distinguish different molecular routes from a sequence change to an observed effect. The supplied manuscript illustrates this value through its reported reconstruction of oncogenic TAL1 variant effects. Such examples establish a technical basis for the ambition, rather than demonstrating comprehensive regulatory decoding.

Conditional downstream possibilities include prioritizing regulatory variants for experiments, selecting informative perturbations and designing sequence changes with desired molecular effects. Reliable prediction of variant combinations would be especially valuable when an individual genome contains many changes whose effects cannot safely be inferred one at a time. These are projected uses of a decoder meeting the proposed scope, not achievements established by the supplied record.

The analogy to reading molecular instructions has limits. Predictive functional interpretation would not by itself supply a complete causal explanation of every regulatory process. Nor would accurate molecular predictions automatically establish disease risk or identify an effective treatment. The manuscript explicitly places broader phenotypes beyond its direct sequence-to-function scope because they involve gene function, development and environmental factors. Clinical prediction and treatment selection would require additional biological models, relevant patient information and separate validation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unresolved capability is dependable quantitative prediction of regulatory consequences across genomes and specified cellular contexts. The AlphaGenome manuscript identifies particular difficulties with distal regulatory elements more than 100 kilobases away, tissue-specific patterns across contexts and condition-specific variant effects. It also reports that personal-genome prediction had not yet been benchmarked. These are documented limitations at the manuscript’s reporting time; they do not establish the absence of a solution throughout the field at a later date.

Engineering synthesis: A broadly useful decoder must connect distant regulatory signals to the correct target genes while preserving quantitative accuracy, and it must represent enough cellular context to distinguish responses to the same sequence in different states or conditions. It must also generalize from its training and benchmark settings to unseen genomes. A long input window alone does not demonstrate that all relevant distant influences have been captured or assigned correctly.

Proposed extensions introduce additional barriers. Structural variants can change the arrangement of regulatory elements and genes, while multiple variants may have interacting effects. A decoder claiming these capabilities would need to represent and evaluate those changes explicitly, rather than relying on performance for isolated variants. It would also need useful uncertainty estimates that identify where predictions are dependable and where a new genome, perturbation or cellular condition exceeds the demonstrated range. These requirements follow from the proposed scope; their field-wide state is not established by the supplied manuscript.

current_state.text: In the supplied AlphaGenome manuscript, the model predicts multiple regulatory measurements and variant effects from 1-megabase DNA segments. Its authors report matching or exceeding the strongest respective available external models on 24 of 26 variant-effect evaluations. This is substantial reported benchmark performance across the evaluated tasks, not evidence of reliable prediction for every regulatory mechanism, complete personal genome or combination of variants.

The manuscript’s Discussion describes remaining challenges in regulation by elements more than 100 kilobases away, tissue-specific patterns and condition-specific variant effects. It explicitly states that personal-genome prediction had not yet been benchmarked. Its reported TAL1 example supports integrated molecular interpretation in a particular setting, while the broader goal of predicting combined changes in real genomes across contexts remains unestablished by the supplied evidence. The review also does not establish performance for structural variants or interacting variants.

The supplied review verifies the manuscript’s identity from its content and directly supports the scientific statements above using saved extracted text. That extraction is partial: it contains 120,000 characters, truncates during page 31 and omits later material. The relevant abstract and Discussion passages were available to the reviewer, but the record does not support conclusions about omitted material. This account relies on that supplied review and does not imply a new inspection of the PDF.

The research associates the manuscript with January 28, 2026 and DOI 10.1038/s41586-025-10014-0, but the validated review did not verify that publication date or DOI association. The source index records retrieval on November 11, 2026; retrieval is not a publication date. Because the supplied freshness record is empty, the evidence does not establish field-wide status on November 1, 2026 or identify subsequent advances. These bibliographic and coverage limits leave the manuscript’s supported reported results intact.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Before experimental results are available, predict expression, splicing and chromatin responses for diverse unseen human genomes and engineered variant combinations across several explicitly specified cell types, states and conditions. Include distant regulatory perturbations and structural variants because they remain within this concept’s scope. The evaluation should test both individual changes and combinations, allowing direct assessment of whether the model captures joint effects.
completion_criteria.label: Prospectively predict molecular responses to unseen genomes and variant combinations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation requirements: Independent laboratories would measure molecular effect sizes and compare them with predictions, including predicted null effects. The protocol would prespecify accuracy, coverage and uncertainty-calibration thresholds, together with the measurements and comparisons used to assess them. No numerical thresholds are supplied here, and these requirements are proposed criteria rather than established community standards. Successful uncertainty estimates should reflect observed prediction errors across the evaluated contexts.
completion_criteria.label: Independent validation meets prespecified accuracy, coverage and calibration thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: Independent evaluations should reproduce performance on held-out genomes and perturbations, report failures as well as successes and state the cellular contexts and variant classes covered. A convincing result would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries; finite tests could not establish literal universality. Claims about disease prediction or treatment selection would require separate demonstrations connecting molecular predictions to biological and clinical outcomes.
completion_criteria.label: Independent evaluations reproduce held-out performance and report practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BIF-04, General reconstruction of causal cellular networks, has the closest explicit overlap. BIF-01 predicts molecular consequences of regulatory sequence in context, whereas BIF-04 seeks causal relationships among cellular components. A decoder could generate hypotheses or predicted perturbation responses for network reconstruction, but predictive accuracy alone would not establish a complete causal network. BIF-03, A transferable, predictive virtual cell, has broader scope: regulatory decoding could supply one component of a model that also represents other cellular processes.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-02, Predictive molecular dynamics from biological sequence, and BIF-09, Proteome-scale prediction of molecular interactions and affinities, concern molecular behavior that could help explain regulatory mechanisms. BIF-01 instead targets regulatory molecular outputs from genomic sequence and context. BIF-06, A general decoder for unknown gene and protein functions, addresses what gene products do; identifying the consequences of changing their regulation does not by itself determine all of those functions.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-05, Computer-aided design of functional whole genomes, and BIF-13, Predictive design of functional genetic circuits and pathways, could use a regulatory decoder to evaluate proposed designs. Their goals also require choosing and constructing functional systems. BIF-01 supplies a prediction capability, which would contribute to design without completing whole-genome, circuit or pathway engineering.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-07, Computational reconstruction of organism-scale molecular maps, concerns the organization of molecular information across an organism, while BIF-08, Reliable reconstruction and forecasting of single-cell fates, concerns cellular trajectories. Regulatory decoding could inform both, but predicting sequence-dependent molecular changes is narrower than reconstructing an organism-scale map or forecasting a cell’s eventual fate.

Roster-based synthesis: BIF-11, Accessible, uncertainty-aware assembly of complex genomes, could provide sequence inputs for regulatory prediction, but reconstructing a genome and interpreting its regulatory consequences are distinct capabilities. BIF-12, Strain-resolved discovery and functional profiling of microbial communities, addresses community composition and function; the present concept’s proposed demonstrations focus on human genomes and specified cellular contexts. BIF-10, A broadly capable autonomous bioinformatics discovery system, could incorporate a regulatory decoder as a specialized tool, while adding broader capabilities for autonomous investigation.

brief.title: Predicting how DNA changes affect cells
possible: Researchers could predict how changes in a person’s DNA alter gene activity in a specified cell type and condition. They could assess changes together, including large DNA rearrangements and combinations whose effects differ from the sum of their separate effects.
The predictions would also cover RNA splicing, how cells assemble RNA messages, and chromatin, the packaging of DNA. This would connect nearby and distant stretches of DNA to their molecular effects.
why: Much of the DNA outside protein-coding genes would become easier to interpret. Researchers could work out which genes a change affects, by how much and in which cells. Predicting several molecular effects together could help explain how a change acts.

Researchers could choose more informative experiments, prioritize DNA changes for testing and design changes with desired molecular effects. Predicting combinations would help them study individual genomes containing many changes.

sources.showed: AlphaGenome predicted several kinds of molecular measurements together and matched or beat leading comparison models on most tests of DNA-change effects.
sources.quote:
AlphaGenome’s ability to simultaneously score
variant effects across all modalities accurately recapitulates the mechanisms of clinically-relevant variants
near the TAL1 oncogene.
sources.cited_for: A model can connect DNA changes to several molecular effects within a shared framework.
sources.not_established: This does not establish reliable predictions for complete individual genomes, interacting changes or arbitrary cellular conditions.

sources.who: Ruchir Rastogi, Aniketh Janardhan Reddy, Ryan Chung and Nilah M. Ioannidis
sources.showed: Additional training on paired personal DNA and gene activity improved predictions for people excluded from training. The improvement applied to genes used in that additional training.
sources.quote: However, fine-tuning does not improve model generalizability to held-out genes, which contain sequences and variants unseen during fine-tuning.
sources.cited_for: Training on personal DNA can improve predictions across people, while transfer to unfamiliar genes remains difficult.
sources.not_established: The improvement did not extend to genes excluded from additional training or establish prediction of interacting DNA changes.

sources.who: Yu Wang, Nan Liang and Ge Gao
sources.showed: SVEN predicted how large DNA changes affect gene activity in different tissues. A small experiment testing DNA deletions supported some predicted effects.
sources.quote: As a sequence-oriented model, SVEN is also able to predict regulatory effects for small noncoding variants.
sources.cited_for: Prediction of large DNA changes has experimental support in a limited setting.
sources.not_established: These results do not establish broad accuracy across molecular effects, cellular conditions and combinations of changes.

sources.who: Layla Siraj, Ryan Tewhey and collaborators
sources.showed: The researchers tested DNA fragments in cells to measure their effects on gene activity. Some nearby changes had combined effects that differed from adding their separate effects.
sources.quote:
We show that this assay effectively
discriminates between likely causal variants and controls, and identified 13,121
regulatory variants with high precision.
sources.cited_for: Experiments can measure many DNA-change effects and reveal interactions that predictions must capture.
sources.not_established: Tests on DNA fragments do not establish predictive accuracy within complete genomes.

sources.who: Connie Huang, Richard W. Shuai, Parth Baokar and collaborators
sources.showed: Models that predicted differences in activity between genes struggled to predict differences between people. They often predicted the wrong direction of change.
sources.quote:
In addition, models often fail to predict the correct direction of
effect of cis-regulatory genetic variation on expression.
sources.cited_for: Success at predicting differences between genes does not establish success at predicting differences between people.
sources.not_established: This evaluation does not determine the performance of AlphaGenome or models developed afterward.

shown: Google DeepMind’s AlphaGenome combines predictions of gene activity, RNA splicing and chromatin measurements. Its reconstruction of cancer-related changes near the TAL1 gene shows how these predictions can support a shared molecular explanation.

Other teams have improved predictions for unfamiliar people and tested effects of large DNA changes. These are partial advances: the broad ability to predict combined changes across individual genomes and cellular conditions remains undemonstrated.
missing: Reliable quantitative predictions must extend to unfamiliar genomes and specified cellular conditions, including effects from distant DNA.
Large DNA rearrangements and interacting changes need explicit tests across gene activity, RNA splicing and chromatin measurements.
Independent experiments must establish accuracy, breadth and uncertainty estimates that reflect actual prediction errors.

milestones.label: Molecular predictions succeed before experiments reveal the answers
milestones.explanation: Predictions would precede experiments on unseen human genomes, combined changes and large rearrangements across cell types, states and conditions, including distant effects. This would test the full intended scope.

milestones.label: Independent tests meet agreed performance thresholds
milestones.explanation: Independent labs would compare measured effects, including no effect, with predictions against preset accuracy, coverage and uncertainty thresholds. This would establish when predictions deserve confidence.

milestones.label: Independent evaluations reproduce results and define their limits
milestones.explanation: Independent evaluations would reproduce performance on genomes and changes excluded from training, reporting failures and the cells and changes covered. This would establish reproducible breadth with clear boundaries.

uncertain: How should a model represent a cell’s state and environmental conditions well enough to distinguish their effects?
What accuracy, coverage and uncertainty thresholds would make the predictions useful, and which experiments should judge them?

page.title: Human regulatory sequence-to-function prediction
page.definition: A sequence-to-function model predicts how human DNA changes alter RNA abundance, RNA splicing—the assembly of RNA segments—and chromatin, the DNA–protein packaging, in a specified cell type, state and condition. It covers distant regulatory elements, structural variants and combinations whose effects are not additive.

goal.need: More than 98% of observed human genetic variation is noncoding. Such variants can change RNA abundance, RNA splicing and chromatin, and their effects can depend on tissue or cell type. Predicting these effects would connect this majority of human variation to experimentally measurable molecular consequences.

statements.context: Recommendation from the workshop held on 28 and 29 July 2014.

statements.context: An objective of the IGVF renewal concept presented to the National Advisory Council for Human Genome Research on 9 September 2024.

completion.title: Independent experiments reproduce regulatory predictions at biological-replicate agreement.
completion.criterion: In blinded experiments independently conducted by two laboratories, a frozen model predicts RNA abundance, splice usage and chromatin changes in held-out human individuals, genes and cellular contexts. Each assay and variant-class stratum attains prediction–measurement agreement at least as high as biological-replicate agreement, using the same prespecified metric. Tests include distal regulatory changes, structural variants and non-additive variant combinations. Achievement applies only to the tested scope.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body was found to have adopted this combined completion test.
completion.basis: NHGRI workshop recommendations, IGVF programme documents, CAGI assessments, DREAM rules, and searches for standards and prizes supplied no completion threshold for this combined capability. This provisional test extends DREAM's comparison with experimental reproducibility to the molecular-prediction goals. Independent experimental replication distinguishes completion from initial validation. The combined requirement is not an IGVF or DREAM standard.

milestones.title: A model finishes first in the Random Promoter DREAM Challenge.
milestones.criterion: Rank first under the organisers' combined Pearson-score and Spearman-score ranking. The challenge used 6,739,258 training promoter sequences and 71,103 test sequences; approximately 87% of the test data were reserved for final evaluation. External training data and ensembles were prohibited. Autosome.org achieved first place in the 2022 challenge, as reported on 11 October 2024. This establishes sequence-to-expression prediction in a yeast reporter system.
milestones.set_by: Random Promoter DREAM Challenge organisers, competition rules and performance-evaluation protocol; this test was written for yeast promoters.
milestones.threshold_quote: We averaged the ranks from both metrics to decide their final ranks.

milestones.title: Genome editing confirms a structural variant's predicted direction of gene-expression change.
milestones.criterion: A predicted expression change caused by a structural variant, a genomic alteration exceeding 50 base pairs, is tested by editing the endogenous locus. The measured change must have the predicted direction and satisfy the experiment's stated significance test. SVEN's study, published on 30 December 2024, tested five selected deletions with CRISPR assays: four directions agreed with predictions and two results were statistically significant. This establishes selected-locus validation, not general structural-variant accuracy.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback based on SVEN's endogenous validation experiments; no external minimum validation rate was found.

milestones.title: Personal-genome expression predictions match linear models on held-out individuals.
milestones.criterion: On identical training and test splits, a sequence model's mean cross-individual Pearson correlation matches the variant-based linear comparators. Rastogi and colleagues used 421 individuals, with 77 test individuals for each of two 200-gene evaluations. Their paper of 25 May 2026 reported mean r = 0.28 on randomly held-out individuals, versus 0.06 for baseline Enformer, with performance comparable to linear models. Fine-tuning did not improve generalization to 670 unseen genes. Cross-individual correlation tests differences between people rather than differences between genes.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback using the published personal-genome comparison protocol; its correlation metric and comparators are external, but no universal acceptance cutoff was found.

milestones.title: A blinded experiment validates the combined decoder at biological-replicate agreement.
milestones.criterion: One blinded experimental study meets the completion test's replicate-agreement comparator for RNA abundance, splice usage and chromatin across held-out individuals, genes and cellular contexts, including distal changes, structural variants and non-additive combinations. Independent experimental replication remains outstanding. AlphaGenome's paper of 28 January 2026 reported matching or exceeding comparators in 25 of 26 variant-effect evaluations, but did not benchmark personal genomes; these results do not establish this combined milestone.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback combining IGVF's generalization and interaction objectives with the experimental-reproducibility comparator used in DREAM assessments; no external combined threshold was found.

not_found: No external completion threshold was found for joint personal-genome, splicing, chromatin, structural-variant and interaction prediction across previously unstudied cellular contexts.
No external minimum validation rate or cross-individual correlation cutoff was found for milestones m2 and m3.
The supplied PDF of Functional dissection of complex trait variants at single-nucleotide resolution could not be opened; its results are not used here.

results.finding: AlphaGenome matched or exceeded comparator models in 24 of 26 variant-effect evaluations.
results.detail: The benchmarks covered multiple regulatory modalities but did not establish agreement at biological-replicate levels in a blinded experiment across the required individuals, genes, contexts and variant classes.
results.quote:
AlphaGenome matched or outperformed the external models on 24 out
of 26 evaluations (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Table 4).

results.finding: Fine-tuned Enformer matched linear models on 77 held-out individuals across 200 genes, with mean cross-individual Pearson r = 0.28.
results.detail: Models used identical individual splits. Fine-tuning did not improve generalization to 670 unseen genes.
results.quote: Our results show that fine-tuning improves expression predictions on held-out individuals, including from held-out populations, for genes seen during fine-tuning, with comparable performance to variant-based linear models commonly used in transcriptome-wide association studies.

results.finding: SVEN predicted the correct expression-change direction for 4 of 5 CRISPR-tested deletions.
results.detail: Two results were statistically significant. The five deletions were selected for predicted strong effects and tested in A375 cells.
results.quote:
SVEN successfully predicted the direction of the impact on gene expression for 4 deletions, and 2 of the results were statistically significant (Fig.
3b and c
, Supplementary Fig.
5b
and
6
).

results.finding: Across 421 individuals and 3,259 genes, four models had mean cross-individual correlation close to zero.
results.detail: The study reports Spearman rather than Pearson correlations. Variant-based linear models explained substantially more cross-individual variation; the text does not establish identical training and test splits.
results.quote:
We also find that, although the mean cross-individual correlation 
is close to zero for all models, there are tails of strongly positively cor-
related and strongly negatively correlated genes for each model (Fig. 1c 
and Extended Data Fig. 3).

results.finding: Autosome.org ranked first in the Random Promoter DREAM Challenge, with 71,103 test sequences.
results.detail: The 2022 yeast reporter challenge used 6,739,258 training sequences and reserved approximately 87% of test data for final evaluation. Final ranks averaged Pearson-score and Spearman-score ranks; external training data and ensembles were prohibited.
results.quote: The competing teams introduced several innovative approaches to solve the expression prediction problem. Autosome.org, the best-performing team, transformed the task into a soft-classification problem by training their network to predict a vector of expression bin probabilities, which was then averaged to yield an estimated expression level, effectively recreating how the data were generated in the experiment.
